title: Kioxia CD9P 7.68TB E3.S NVMe SSD Review Fast Gen5 Storage
gist: Kioxia's CD9P is a PCIe Gen5 E3.S enterprise NVMe SSD family reviewed here at 7.68TB (read-intensive -R variant); the author argues it may be the last data-center SSD generation available in both U.2 and EDSFF form factors, since PCIe Gen6 drives will require EDSFF electrically.

themes.theme: CD9P Product Lineup: Capacity vs. Endurance Tradeoff

insights.claim: Kioxia's CD9P read-intensive (-R) variant offers 7.68TB of capacity rated at 1 drive-write-per-day (DWPD) for 5 years, while the mixed-use (-V) variant trades capacity down to 6.4TB in exchange for 3x higher endurance (3 DWPD).
insights.speaker: Eric Smith
insights.so_what: Enterprise buyers must pick the variant matched to workload write intensity - -R for read-heavy/cold storage capacity plays, -V for higher-write workloads at a meaningful capacity discount.
insights.locator: That "-R" tells us we have the read-intensive version

insights.claim: Kioxia rates the CD9P, which uses its BiCS8 NAND, for up to 14.8GB/s sequential read, 7GB/s sequential write, 2.6M random read IOPS, and 450K random write IOPS at 4K block size.
insights.speaker: Eric Smith
insights.so_what: These are vendor-claimed specs from the summary slide, not yet validated against measured benchmarks in this article - useful as a baseline to compare once real performance results are published.
insights.locator: Other major specs are that we expect to see 14.8GB/s read

themes.theme: EDSFF vs. U.2: An Approaching Form-Factor Cutover

insights.claim: The author argues the CD9P may be the last data-center SSD generation available in either U.2 or EDSFF (E3.S/E1) form factors, because PCIe Gen6 drives will electrically require EDSFF, forcing the industry off the legacy SAS-compatible U.2 connector.
insights.speaker: Eric Smith
insights.so_what: Signals a hard form-factor cutover coming with PCIe Gen6 enterprise SSDs; server and storage vendors still standardized on U.2 should plan for a forced EDSFF transition industry-wide.
insights.quote: starting with PCIe Gen6 drives, electrically it seems like we need EDSFF instead of the older U.2 connector
insights.locator: For some context here, we discussed some time ago how E1 and E3 EDSFF

insights.claim: The E3.S form factor enables higher storage density than U.2 through thinner carrier trays and a smaller PCIe Gen5 x4 connector, which also improves cooling and signal integrity versus the older U.2 connector.
insights.speaker: Eric Smith
insights.so_what: Density and thermal/signal advantages favor continued E3.S/EDSFF adoption in space- and power-constrained data center storage nodes.
insights.locator: Perhaps the biggest change is the connector

insights.claim: Despite EDSFF's density advantages, U.2 still offers higher maximum single-drive capacity today: the CD9P spans 1.6TB to 30.72TB in E3.S but reaches 61.44TB in the 15mm U.2 form factor, which has more internal volume for NAND package placement.
insights.speaker: Eric Smith
insights.so_what: For buyers maximizing single-drive capacity today, U.2 still outperforms E3.S - a nuance to weigh even as the industry migrates toward EDSFF standardization.
insights.locator: As for specs, this drive ranges from 1.6TB to 30.72TB
